metaDescription: Six BLACK+DECKER food processors and choppers compared by motor power, bowl size, discs and controls, so you can pick the right one for your kitchen.
expertTake: If you want one BLACK+DECKER that actually replaces chopping by hand, buy the 8 Cup 450W with touchpad: it is the sweet spot of bowl size, motor and washable controls. The best value is the plain 8 cup twin, and batch cooks should look at the 10 cup PowerPro for its wider feed chute. Choose the 3 cup chopper only if your jobs are herbs, onions and small dips. Anyone who kneads dough regularly or cooks for a large household should skip this brand's lineup and shop full-size 12 to 14 cup machines instead.
introParagraphs: A food processor is a motor-driven bowl with interchangeable cutting tools, and the right size depends less on a brand name than on how you cook. A small chopper and a full processor share a look on the shelf, but they differ in motor power, bowl volume and the discs that slice and shred, and that is where buyers get disappointed.

This guide explains how the BLACK+DECKER range divides into chopper and processor classes, what the wattage and cup numbers really mean, and which version suits a given kitchen. The top picks are above, and the detailed reviews below show who each machine fits and who should look elsewhere.

products.name: BLACK+DECKER 8-Cup Food Processor, 450W with Touchpad

specList.label: Locking
specList.value: Lid acts as the bowl lock

products.description:
This is the BLACK+DECKER most households should buy. An 8 cup bowl is the size where a food processor starts doing real kitchen work: a batch of salsa, a full head of cabbage for slaw, a block of cheese or a double batch of hummus. The 450 watt motor drives a stainless S-blade for chopping and pureeing and a reversible metal disc that slices on one side and shreds on the other. The design goal is easy assembly, since the lid doubles as the locking mechanism, so you set the bowl on the base and the act of closing the lid engages the interlock.

The controls are the difference from its sibling listing. Touchpad low, high and pulse buttons wipe clean with one pass of a cloth, where raised buttons collect splatter. Compared with the 150 watt 1.5 cup chopper, it has three times the motor wattage and more than five times the bowl, so it tackles raw carrots, hard cheese and dough-like mixtures that would stall a mini chopper. It does not have the work-bowl size or motor of a 14 cup full-size machine, and it is a countertop appliance for weeknight prep rather than a daily-batch machine.

Ownership is straightforward. The bowl, lid, pusher, blade and disc are removable and are listed as dishwasher safe on the family, though blades last longer if hand washed and dried. Store the discs in the bowl or a drawer so the edges do not get nicked. Processing hard cheese in short pulses rather than a long run keeps the motor cooler, and loading the bowl no higher than the S-blade shaft reduces lid leakage with liquid-heavy recipes.
products.bestFor: Households that want one full-featured processor for chopping, shredding and slicing without a large footprint.
pros: 8 cup bowl handles salsa, slaw and hummus in single batches
450W motor outpaces the chopper-class units in this family
Wipe-clean touchpad with low, high and pulse settings
Lid-as-lock assembly makes setup quick and low in fuss
cons: Not built for heavy dough or continuous large-batch use
Plastic body and bowl scratch and stain with tomato and curry

products.name: BLACK+DECKER 8-Cup Food Processor, 450W Easy Assembly

specList.label: Assembly
specList.value: Lid acts as the locking mechanism

products.description:
This listing is the same 450 watt, 8 cup design as the top pick, described without the touchpad detail, so treat the two as near-twins and let availability and control style decide. It is the stripped-down version of the family: S-blade, reversible shred and slice disc, and the same lid-locking idea that avoids fighting a twist-lock bowl. That makes it ideal for someone who wants a food processor for salsa, shredded cheese and chopped vegetables, and nothing more elaborate.

The trade is in the controls. Where the touchpad model gives you low, high and pulse, this listing simply describes a powerful 450 watt motor and the basic cutting functions, so check the product page before you buy to confirm the control layout you are getting. In the same lineup, it sits between the 3 cup chopper, which is better for herbs and small prep, and the 10 cup wide-mouth model, which has a larger bowl and a wider feed chute.

Practical ownership is the same as the top pick. Wash the removable parts promptly, because garlic and onion odors cling to plastic bowls, and avoid running the S-blade empty or on hard items like whole nuts for long, which dulls the edge. A 450 watt direct-drive motor suits intermittent household work; give it short rests when you are shredding a lot of cheese or chopping root vegetables in several batches.
products.bestFor: Anyone who wants the family's 8 cup size and 450W motor with minimal fuss.
pros: 8 cup bowl and 450W motor match the top pick for the same jobs
Reversible disc gives both slicing and shredding in one piece

products.name: BLACK+DECKER PowerPro Wide-Mouth 10-Cup Food Processor FP2500B
products.description:
The PowerPro FP2500B is the largest bowl in the BLACK+DECKER lineup and the one to pick if you do bigger batches. Ten cups gives roughly a quarter more working volume than the 8 cup models, and the wide-mouth feed chute is the feature that actually saves time: a wider opening takes a whole potato, a block of cheese or half a pepper without pre-cutting, which means fewer stops and less knife work. Two speeds and a pulse give a little more control than a plain on-off processor.

The listing does not state a motor wattage in the data we reviewed, so we cannot rank its power against the 450 watt models, and that is worth keeping in mind. Larger bowls with a modest motor can struggle with thick mixtures such as dense dips, because the blade has more load to move. If your cooking is mostly slicing and shredding, the wide chute is a bigger benefit than raw power; if it is mostly pureeing hard ingredients, the 450 watt 8 cup units have a known number to lean on.

The soft-touch Mylar buttons are sealed membranes, easy to wipe but less satisfying than physical switches, and they can wear at the edges with age. Keep the control panel dry and wipe it rather than submerging the base. This is an older design, so spare parts and accessories are worth checking for before you buy, particularly the discs, which are the pieces most likely to chip.
products.bestFor: Larger families and batch cooks who want a wider feed chute and a 10 cup bowl.
pros: 10 cup bowl is the largest in the BLACK+DECKER lineup
Wide-mouth feed chute takes bigger pieces with less pre-cutting
Two speeds and pulse give more control than plain on-off
Sealed soft-touch buttons wipe clean quickly
cons: No motor wattage stated, so power versus the 450W models is unknown
Older platform makes spare discs and parts worth checking first

products.name: BLACK+DECKER 8-Cup Food Processor FP1600B
products.description:
The FP1600B is the traditional version of the 8 cup BLACK+DECKER, with a conventional feed chute and pusher, a slicing and shredding disc, and a stainless blade. A pusher on a feed chute is a small safety and control feature that matters more than it sounds: it guides food down toward the spinning disc in a straight line and keeps fingers out, which gives more even slices than dropping the food in by hand. A safety interlock means the blades only run when the lid is secured to the bowl.

The listing gives no motor wattage in the data we reviewed, so unlike the 450 watt models we cannot state its power, and the description is shorter on detail than its siblings. That is a reason to treat it as a basic, reliable older design rather than the most capable option. Next to the 3 cup HC300B chopper it is the one to buy if you want slicing and shredding discs, which the chopper lacks entirely.

Take care of it like any plastic-bowl processor. Parts are listed as dishwasher safe, but a top-rack wash is kinder to the plastic and to the blade edge. Do not let the bowl stand with turmeric or tomato sauce, which stain permanently, and always feed the pusher slowly rather than forcing food, since a stall puts load on the motor.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want an 8 cup bowl with a classic feed chute and pusher and do not need the touchpad.
pros: Feed chute with pusher gives straighter, more even slices
Safety interlock stops the blade unless the lid is locked
Slicing and shredding disc included in the 8 cup package
Removable parts are listed as dishwasher safe
cons: Motor wattage is not stated, so power cannot be compared
Plainer feature set than the 450W touchpad version

products.name: BLACK+DECKER 3-Cup Electric Food Chopper HC300B, 175W
products.description:
The HC300B is a food chopper, not a full processor, and it has a clear role: small jobs that a knife would take five minutes to do. A 175 watt motor spins bi-level stainless blades, two stacked sets of cutting edges that chop the top and bottom of the bowl contents in the same run, which is a design used to solve the common mini-chopper problem of a mushy bottom and chunky top. One-touch pulse control puts the texture in your hand: tap for coarse, hold for fine.

Its oil holes are the practical standout. Drip oil through the lid while the blades turn and you can make hummus, mayonnaise-style emulsions and vinaigrettes without lifting the lid and making a mess. Compared with the 1.5 cup chopper in this family, the extra capacity and 25 additional watts handle a full onion, a handful of nuts or a batch of dip rather than a clove or two, and compared with the 8 cup processors it takes up a fraction of the counter space but cannot slice or shred.

Care is simple, since the bowl, lid and blades are dishwasher safe. Do not run it continuously beyond short bursts; a small motor is built for pulses, and overheating shows as a hot smell. Cut hard foods into roughly half-inch cubes before chopping, and keep fingers away from the stacked blades, which are sharp even when the unit looks idle.
products.bestFor: Small kitchens and cooks who mostly chop herbs, onions, nuts and make small batches of dips.
pros: Bi-level blades chop top and bottom layers evenly
Oil holes allow adding oil to dips without opening the lid
3 cup bowl handles an onion or a small dip batch
Dishwasher-safe parts and one-touch pulse keep use simple
cons: 175W motor cannot shred, slice or handle dense dough
Small bowl needs batching for family-size recipes

products.name: BLACK+DECKER 1.5-Cup Electric Food Chopper, 150W
products.description:
This is the smallest machine in the family and a sensible choice for one or two people. A 1.5 cup bowl is enough for chopped herbs, breadcrumbs, a few cloves of garlic or a small portion of salsa, and the 150 watt motor with bi-level stainless blades does those jobs quickly in a few pulses. The oil holes in the lid make it useful for small batches of vinaigrette or hummus, which is a feature you rarely find on a chopper this small.

The limitation is obvious and should be stated plainly: it is a chopper, and it cannot replace a food processor. Its motor is 150 watts, well below the 450 watts of the 8 cup models, and its bowl holds one fifth of theirs. Pushing in dense ingredients like raw carrots or hard cheese will stall it or wear it down. Within the family, choose the 3 cup HC300B if you cook for more than two people and you want extra volume at a small cost in footprint.

Upkeep is minimal: the bowl, lid and blade are removable and dishwasher safe. Pulse in short bursts, shake the bowl between pulses to move food toward the blades and let the unit rest after a minute of work. Store it with the blade assembly removed to avoid dulling and accidental cuts when you reach into a drawer.
products.bestFor: Singles and couples who want to chop herbs, garlic and small amounts of dip with minimal storage.
pros: 150W motor and 1.5 cup bowl suit herbs, garlic and breadcrumbs
Bi-level stay-sharp blades work evenly in a small bowl
Oil holes make tiny batches of dressing and hummus easy
Compact base stores in a drawer or small cabinet
cons: Cannot slice, shred or process dense food like hard cheese
Bowl is small, so family-size recipes need several batches

buyingCriteria.explanation: A chopper is a short bowl with a fixed blade and a small motor; a processor adds a feed chute, slicing and shredding discs and a stronger motor. Within this brand the 1.5 cup unit at 150 watts and the 3 cup HC300B at 175 watts are choppers, while the 8 cup models at 450 watts and the 10 cup PowerPro are processors. Buyers often order a chopper expecting to shred a block of cheese and learn the hard way that no disc is included. Decide first which tasks you need: if the list includes shredding or slicing, only the 8 and 10 cup models qualify.

Wattage is a rough proxy for torque, and torque is what moves the blade through dense food without stalling. The 450 watt 8 cup models have three times the stated power of the 150 watt chopper, which is the difference between pureeing cooked beans and burning out the motor on a raw carrot. Treat watts as a comparison within a brand, not a promise, since the FP1600B and FP2500B do not state a figure in the data we reviewed. If a listing leaves out wattage, assume modest power and favor light, intermittent jobs.

Cup capacity is the full brim volume, and a useful working volume is closer to half to two thirds for liquids and a little more for dry chopping. An 8 cup bowl really holds about 5 cups of salsa-type mix without leaking at the shaft, while the 10 cup PowerPro gives a little more headroom. Match the bowl to your largest regular recipe, not a once-a-year one. If you cook for one or two, the 1.5 or 3 cup choppers avoid the problem of food spreading thin across a large bowl, which leaves it unevenly chopped.

The feed chute decides how much pre-cutting you do. A wide-mouth chute like the one on the FP2500B takes a whole potato or half a head of cabbage, while a narrow chute means slicing food to fit. The pusher lets you apply steady pressure for even slices and keeps fingers away from the disc. A common mistake is pushing too hard, which stalls the motor and gives uneven cuts; let the disc do the work and use a firm, steady, light push.

Raised buttons trap splatter in the crevices, while a touchpad or sealed membrane wipes clean in one pass. The 450 watt touchpad model has low, high and pulse, the FP2500B has two speeds plus pulse on soft-touch buttons, and the choppers have a single pulse. Pulse is the control that matters most, because it lets you stop at the texture you want; a processor that only runs on or off will over-process. Remember that dishwasher-safe plastics still stain and cloud over time, so hand wash when you can.

Processors have a lid interlock so the blade cannot spin unless the lid is fully locked. The 450 watt models use the lid itself as the lock, and the FP1600B lists an interlocking system that requires a secured lid. This matters for safety and for ease: a bowl that is hard to lock gets used less. Always remove the blade by the center post and never put hands in the bowl while the machine is plugged in, since S-blades keep their edge for years.

specDecoder.meaning: A stated electrical input or output rating for the motor. More watts generally means more torque for dense foods, though design and gearing matter too.
specDecoder.watchFor: Compare watts only within a brand and class. The 450 watt 8 cup and the 150 watt chopper are far apart, and several listings here do not state watts at all.

specDecoder.meaning: The brim-full volume of the work bowl. Usable volume for liquids is much lower because the center post and blade take space and liquids leak up the shaft.
specDecoder.watchFor: An 8 cup bowl is best filled to about two thirds for wet mixtures. Do not read 10 cups on the PowerPro as 10 cups of soup.

specDecoder.meaning: A two-prong stainless blade shaped like an S that chops and purees as it spins around the center post.
specDecoder.watchFor: A stay-sharp or bi-level claim, as on the choppers, is about blade stacking rather than edge hardness. Hand wash it to preserve the edge.

specDecoder.meaning: A momentary control that runs the motor only while pressed, letting you stop at the texture you want.
specDecoder.watchFor: Choppers like the HC300B rely on pulse alone. If a processor lacks pulse, it is easy to over-process into paste.

specDecoder.meaning: A mechanical switch that blocks motor operation unless the lid is fully seated and locked.
specDecoder.watchFor: It protects fingers, but it can wear. If the machine runs without the lid locked or refuses to start, stop using it.

howWeEvaluated.title: Class and capability fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We first sorted the BLACK+DECKER lineup into choppers and processors, because the jobs they do barely overlap. The 1.5 cup and 3 cup models sit in the first class, and the 8 and 10 cup models in the second. Each pick is judged inside its own class so a chopper is not penalized for lacking discs.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor power and data completeness
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated wattage across the lineup, placing the 450 watt 8 cup models above the 175 watt and 150 watt choppers, and marking the FP1600B and FP2500B as unknown because their listings do not state a figure. Missing data lowered confidence in a pick's ranking rather than being filled with guesses.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cutting tools and feed design
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at what each machine actually cuts with: the S-blade, the reversible slice and shred disc, the wide-mouth chute on the FP2500B and the pusher on the FP1600B. Machines with discs and a wide chute scored higher on versatility, since they replace more knife work.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ease of cleaning and assembly
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on the spec sheet and owner feedback patterns, we weighed lid-as-lock assembly, wipe-clean touchpad or sealed controls, and dishwasher-safe removable parts. The touchpad 450 watt model gained for easy cleaning, and the choppers for having few parts to wash.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value inside the family
howWeEvaluated.description: Value was judged among BLACK+DECKER models only, because the question is which version of this brand to buy. The 8 cup 450 watt pair offers the best balance, the 3 cup HC300B is the efficient choice for small jobs, and the 10 cup PowerPro is best only when a wider chute and bigger bowl are the priority.

cards.label: Chopper
cards.text: A short bowl, a single blade and a small motor. It excels at herbs, garlic, onions, nuts and small dips. In this lineup it means the 1.5 cup 150 watt model and the 3 cup 175 watt HC300B. They do not slice or shred and cannot handle dense dough.

cards.label: Food processor
cards.text: A taller bowl with a feed chute and discs that slice and shred, powered by a stronger motor. It does all the chopper's jobs in a larger batch and adds shredded cheese, sliced vegetables and slaw. Here that means the two 450 watt 8 cup models, the FP1600B and the 10 cup FP2500B.

howToChoose.note: Pick a chopper if you only chop small amounts and want tiny storage. Pick a processor if you ever shred cheese or prep vegetables in bulk.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Salsa wants a pulse control so tomatoes and onions stay in pieces rather than turning to liquid. Hummus needs a stronger motor for thick chickpea paste and a way to add oil while running.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The 8 cup 450 watt touchpad model is the best for salsa because of low, high and pulse. For small hummus batches the HC300B with its oil holes is the easiest, while larger batches belong in the 450 watt 8 cup bowl.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You shred cheese or slice vegetables weekly and cook for four or more people. Then the 450 watt 8 cup touchpad model or the 10 cup PowerPro justify the bigger footprint.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You mainly chop herbs, onions and small dips. The 1.5 cup chopper or the 3 cup HC300B does the work, and a bigger processor would sit unused in a cabinet.

maintenance.task: Hand wash the blade and discs
maintenance.why: Stainless edges dull faster in a dishwasher and the blade holder can loosen. Washing by hand keeps slicing discs flat and sharp.
A worn interlock can fail to engage or fail to disengage. If the machine starts with the lid unlocked, stop using it.
Splatter in the controls seeps into buttons over time. Wipe with a damp cloth and never submerge the motor base.

maintenance.task: Inspect the bowl and lid for cracks
maintenance.why: Plastic crazes with heat and dishwasher cycles. A cracked bowl leaks and a cracked lid can fail the interlock.
Small motors heat up with continuous use. A minute of rest between batches prevents overload cutouts and extends life.
Loose discs nick and dull in drawers. Keep them in the bowl or a disc holder.

faq.q: Which BLACK+DECKER food processor is best overall?
faq.a: For most households, the 8 cup 450 watt model with touchpad controls is the best balance. It has enough bowl for family cooking, a motor powerful enough for cheese and root vegetables and cleaner controls. If you cook in large batches, the 10 cup PowerPro with its wide feed chute is the upgrade.

faq.q: What is the difference between a chopper and a food processor?
faq.a: A chopper is a small bowl with a blade and a modest motor, best for herbs, onions and small dips. A food processor adds a feed chute and slice and shred discs and has a stronger motor. If you need to shred cheese or slice cucumbers, you need a processor.

faq.q: Can a BLACK+DECKER processor knead dough?
faq.a: The 8 and 10 cup models are not built for bread dough, which is thick and heavy and can overload a small motor. Light pastry or pizza dough in small batches is possible with a processor, but a stand mixer is the safer choice. The choppers are not suitable at all.
The BLACK+DECKER listings state dishwasher-safe removable parts. Top-rack washing is gentler, and hand washing the blade and discs protects the edges. Never put the motor base in water.

faq.q: Is a bigger bowl always better?
faq.a: No. Large bowls spread small quantities thinly, which leaves food unevenly chopped, and they take more storage. Match the bowl to your regular recipes: 1.5 or 3 cups for small prep and 8 to 10 cups for family cooking.

faq.q: How long should I run it at a time?
faq.a: Use short pulses rather than continuous runs. Small motors heat quickly, and a minute of work followed by a rest is a safe habit. If you smell hot plastic or the motor slows, stop and let it cool.
